items.prompt: Read this speech aloud as if you were giving it in assembly. Use pauses and emphasis to persuade your audience.

criteria.label: Reads fluently and accurately
Uses pauses and emphasis to persuade
Changes tone for the question and for the serious points
Sounds confident and sincere

items.readText:
Good morning, everyone. My name is Arya, and I would like to be your next school council representative.
Our school is a wonderful place, but I know we can make it even better. Have you ever waited ten minutes to borrow a football at break? I have. That is why my first promise is simple: a sports box for every class.
My second promise is a suggestion box outside the library, so that every pupil, from Grade 1 to Grade 6, can share ideas.
I will listen carefully, and I will keep the promises I make today. Thank you.
hints: Read the speech silently first and mark the words you want to stress.
Pause after the question so the audience can think.
items.explanation: A persuasive speech is more powerful when the speaker pauses after key points, stresses important words and sounds sincere.

items.prompt: Give a one-minute opening speech for or against this motion: Homework should be optional for primary pupils.

criteria.label: States a clear position on the motion
Gives at least two reasons with examples
Uses persuasive language, including a rhetorical question
Speaks clearly at a good pace
Ends with a strong summary

hints: Begin by saying clearly whether you are for or against the motion.
Signpost your reasons: firstly, secondly, finally.
Finish by repeating your position in one strong sentence.
items.explanation: An opening speech in a debate states a position, supports it with reasons and examples and ends with a clear summary.

items.prompt: Give a short talk explaining why Indonesia has a wet season and a dry season. Your audience is a class of Grade 4 pupils.

criteria.label: Explains the main cause clearly in simple words
Describes the steps in the right order
Uses vocabulary that suits younger listeners
Speaks clearly and keeps the audience interested

hints: Explain one idea at a time: land and sea, then the wind, then the rain.
Replace difficult words with simple ones, or explain them.
items.explanation: A good explanation for younger pupils breaks the process into simple steps and uses words they understand.

items.prompt: Your opponent says: School uniforms stop pupils from expressing themselves. Respond politely, explain why you disagree and give evidence.

criteria.label: Sums up the opponent’s point fairly
Disagrees politely, with phrases such as I understand, however
Gives a clear counter-argument with an example
Stays calm and confident

hints: Start by showing that you have listened: I understand that...
Then give your counter-argument and one example.
items.explanation: A good rebuttal shows respect for the other side, then explains clearly why the point is weak, using evidence.

items.prompt: Tell the same news twice: first to a friend, then to your head teacher. The news is that your class has won a recycling competition.

criteria.label: Uses informal, friendly language with the friend
Uses formal, polite language with the head teacher
Gives the key facts both times
Changes tone of voice to suit each listener

hints: Plan the facts first: what you won, when and how.
Think about greetings: Guess what! for a friend, Good morning for a head teacher.
items.explanation: Speakers change their words and tone for different listeners. The facts stay the same, but the register changes.

items.prompt: Give a short vote of thanks to a visiting author at a school assembly. Mention one thing you learned from the visit.

criteria.label: Uses formal language suitable for an assembly
Thanks the visitor by name and mentions specific details
Is short, clear and well organised
Speaks warmly and confidently

hints: A vote of thanks is short: thank the visitor, mention a highlight and thank them again.
Use the visitor’s name and title.
items.explanation: A vote of thanks is a short, formal speech that thanks a guest and shows that the audience valued the visit.

items.prompt: Argue both sides. Speak for one minute for this motion, then one minute against it: Every school should have a vegetable garden.

criteria.label: Gives strong reasons for the motion
Gives strong reasons against the motion
Uses clear signposts such as firstly and on the other hand
Keeps a fair, confident tone on both sides
Finishes within the time

hints: Plan two reasons for each side before you start.
Use a clear signal when you switch sides, such as On the other hand.
items.explanation: Arguing both sides helps you understand an issue fully and prepares you to answer an opponent in a real debate.

items.prompt: Which phrase is best for politely challenging an opponent in a debate?

options.text: I understand my opponent’s point; however, the evidence shows something different.
That’s rubbish and everyone knows it.
options.why: This is rude and gives no evidence.

options.text: Whatever. Next point.
options.why: This ignores the opponent’s argument.

options.text: My opponent is wrong because I say so.
options.why: This gives no reason or evidence.

hints: Good debaters are polite even when they disagree.
A strong challenge recognises the other point, then gives evidence.
Find the option that mentions evidence.
items.explanation: The best challenge shows you listened, then uses evidence to disagree. This is more persuasive than rudeness.

items.prompt: Put the stages of a school debate in order.
items: The first speaker for the motion speaks.
The first speaker against the motion speaks.
Each side gives a closing summary.
hints: A debate begins by stating what will be discussed.
Each side speaks in turn before anyone sums up.
Start with the person who runs the debate.
items.explanation: The chair introduces the motion, each side opens, speakers answer each other, each side sums up and finally the audience votes.

items.prompt: You are speaking to parents at a formal school event. Which sentence is most suitable?

options.text: Hey everyone, cool that you turned up!
options.why: This is too casual for a formal event.

options.text: You lot should look at our projects.
options.why: You lot is informal and sounds rude.

options.text: Thank you all for coming this evening to see our science projects.
Um, so, yeah, the projects are over there.
options.why: This sounds unprepared.

hints: Think about who the audience is and how formal the event is.
Formal speech is polite, clear and complete.
Find the sentence that thanks the audience politely.
items.explanation: At a formal event, a speaker should be polite and clear. Thanking the audience for coming is a good, formal start.

items.prompt: In a debate speech, what is a claim?

options.text: a joke to start the speech
options.why: Jokes may begin a speech, but they are not the claim.

options.text: your main point or position
a question to your opponent
options.why: This is a challenge, not your main point.

options.text: a thank you to the audience
options.why: This is polite, but it is not the claim.

hints: The claim is what you want the audience to believe.
Think of the central idea of your speech.
It answers the question: what is my argument?
items.explanation: A claim is the main point you want to prove.

items.prompt: Sort each sentence into claim or evidence.

items.text: Trees can cool a school by degrees.
A survey showed readers score higher.

hints: A claim is an opinion or position.
Evidence is a fact, example or statistic.
Ask: could this be checked?
items.explanation: Claims say what should happen. Evidence gives facts or examples to support the claim.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a short debate speech in order.
hints: Start with a polite greeting.
State the main point before supporting it.
Finish by summing up.
items.explanation: A clear speech greets the audience, states a claim, gives evidence, answers the opposition and closes with a summary.

items.prompt: Which line is an example of a rhetorical question?

options.text: We will plant, we will water, we will care.
options.why: This uses repetition, not a question.

options.text: Clean, safe and green.
options.why: This is a list of three.

options.text: Who wants to swim in a dirty river?
You can make a difference today.
options.why: This speaks directly to the audience.

hints: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get an answer.
Look for a line ending in a question mark.
Which line makes the audience think without needing a reply?
items.explanation: A rhetorical question makes the audience think and does not need an answer.

items.prompt: Build a polite closing to a speech. Use the cards.
items.answer: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for listening.
hints: A formal closing is polite.
It starts by addressing the audience.
Put the phrase thank you for listening last.
items.explanation: A formal speech closes by addressing the audience politely and thanking them.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a rebuttal? The motion is: School should end at 3 pm.

options.text: My opponent says pupils are tired, but a short break would solve that problem.
School should end at 3 pm because pupils are tired.
options.why: This is a claim, not a rebuttal.

options.text: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this debate.
options.why: This is a greeting.

options.text: In conclusion, I believe I am right.
options.why: This is a closing, not a rebuttal.

hints: A rebuttal responds to the other side.
It often refers to what the opponent said.
Look for the sentence that answers an opposing point.
items.explanation: A rebuttal answers the other side, using the opponent’s point and giving a counter-argument.

items.prompt: Name the device. Can we really ignore the problem any longer? Write rhetorical question, repetition or rule of three.
hints: The sentence is a question, but the speaker does not expect an answer.
It makes the audience think.
One of the three options is a question.
items.explanation: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not to get an answer.

items.prompt: Choose all the phrases that introduce evidence.

options.text: I just feel that ...
options.why: This gives a feeling, not evidence.

options.text: For example, ...
Statistics show that ...
According to a recent survey, ...
Everybody knows that ...
options.why: This is a vague claim without proof.

hints: Evidence needs a fact, example or source.
Look for phrases that point to something checkable.
Which ones refer to data or examples?
items.explanation: For example, according to a survey and statistics all introduce checkable information.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest piece of evidence for the claim that cycling helps health?

options.text: I think cycling is fun.
options.why: A feeling is not evidence.

options.text: A study found that children who cycle daily have stronger hearts.
My friend likes cycling.
options.why: A single friend’s liking is weak.

options.text: Everyone says cycling is good.
options.why: This is vague with no source.

hints: Strong evidence is specific.
A study is better than a feeling.
Look for the answer that gives a clear result.
items.explanation: A study with a specific finding is strong evidence. The other answers are opinions or vague.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by their job in a debate speech.

items.text: Breaks do not waste time: they help us.
Clubs are not costly: many are free.

hints: A claim is the main point.
Evidence supports the claim.
A rebuttal answers the opponent.
items.explanation: Claims say what should happen, evidence supports them, and rebuttals respond to the other side.

items.prompt: Read: We need clean air. We need clean water. We need clean streets. Which device is used?

options.text: repetition and rule of three
rhetorical question
options.why: No question is asked.

options.text: simile
options.why: No comparison with like or as is used.

options.text: direct address
options.why: The speaker does not use you.

hints: Look for something that repeats.
Count how many items are in the list.
The same pattern is used three times.
items.explanation: The repeated pattern We need clean ... appears three times, which is repetition and a rule of three.

items.prompt: Sort each line by the device it uses.

items.text: Who would choose a dirty beach?
We care, we care, we care.

hints: Look for a question first.
Count the words in a list.
Direct address speaks to you.
items.explanation: A question that needs no answer is rhetorical. A list of three is the rule of three. Speaking to you is direct address. Repeated words show repetition.

items.prompt: Your opponent says: Homework helps children learn. Which is the best rebuttal?

options.text: That is a silly thing to say.
options.why: This attacks the speaker, not the argument.

options.text: I disagree because I do not like homework.
options.why: This is only a personal feeling.

options.text: Homework can help, but a study showed that too much leaves children tired, so a smaller amount is better.
Homework is homework.
options.why: This repeats words and gives no argument.

hints: A rebuttal answers the point with a reason.
Do not attack the person.
Look for the answer with a reason and evidence.
items.explanation: A strong rebuttal accepts what is fair, then gives a reason and evidence for a different view.

items.prompt: Which closing is best for a debate speech?

options.text: Also, I forgot to say that trees are tall.
options.why: A closing should not add new weak points.

options.text: I have no more to say.
options.why: This does not sum up or persuade.

options.text: Thanks. Bye.
options.why: This does not give a summary.

options.text: To sum up, we should plant more trees because they clean the air and cool our schools. Please vote for this motion.

hints: A closing summarises the main points.
It may end with a call to action.
Avoid adding new arguments.
items.explanation: A strong closing sums up the key points and asks the audience to act, here with the vote.
